prompt:
Pixel-art sprite sheet, single image, fully transparent background.

SUBJECT: the undead zombie basketball player in the attached reference image.
Match that character exactly: sickly grey-green skin, ragged mid-brown hair,
sunken eyes with small pale pupils, a lipless grin showing the teeth, dark
rotted patches on the arms and legs, a torn and ragged blue sleeveless
basketball jersey with a yellow number 13, torn blue shorts with white and
yellow trim, white high-top sneakers with blue and yellow flashes over white
socks. Identical colours, identical proportions, identical build and identical
height as the reference, in every frame.

LAYOUT: one horizontal row of 5 frames of equal width, evenly spaced. No
borders, no frame numbers, no labels, no background, no drop shadows.

POSE GUIDE: TWO images are attached, and they do different jobs.

The CHARACTER REFERENCE -- the finished pixel-art drawing of the character --
is the only authority on WHO HE IS. His colours, his proportions, his build,
his height, his face, his kit and the drawing style all come from that image
and from the SUBJECT above, and nothing below changes any of them.

The other image is a POSE GUIDE: a stick-figure diagram on a plain white
background, five figures in a row on one ground line, in the same left-to-right
order as the FRAMES listed below. The Nth figure in the pose guide is the pose
for the Nth frame. Take the GEOMETRY from it and only the geometry: where each
foot is, which foot is on the ground line and which is lifted, how each knee is
bent, the angle of each shoe, how far his body leans forward and how his back
curves, how the shoulder line tilts, how high the dribbling hand is and how far
ahead of him it reaches, where the swinging free hand is, and which way his
head is turned. Where the words below and the pose guide describe the same
thing, they agree; the pose guide is the exact version of it.

THE COLOURS ON THE POSE GUIDE ONLY TELL THE LIMBS APART, so that where his legs
cross you can see which is which. He runs toward the LEFT edge with his chest
turned toward the viewer, so his dribbling side is the side FURTHER from the
viewer: RED is the dribbling arm, reaching ahead of him on the far side of his
body; ORANGE is the leg on that same far side; BLUE is the free arm, on the
side NEARER the viewer; GREEN is the leg on that near side. None of these
colours belongs in the drawing: his skin, his kit and his shoes keep exactly
the colours of the character reference.

THE HANDS ON THE POSE GUIDE: the FLAT hand with its fingers spread is the
dribbling hand, palm to the floor, at exactly that height. The small closed
square at the end of the blue arm is the free hand, a loose fist, swinging as
he runs. The dribbling hand never pumps like a sprinter's: it stays out ahead
of him, pushing the ball down.

THE HEAD ON THE POSE GUIDE: the TRIANGLE on the face is his nose, and it points
the way he is looking -- toward the LEFT edge, the way he is running. The
curved line down the face bulges the same way, and the small oval on the other
side of the head is the ear that shows. HE IS NOT LOOKING BACK OVER HIS
SHOULDER AND NOT LOOKING AT THE VIEWER: he looks where he is going, the same
way in all five frames. The short lines on top are his hair sticking out at
rest.

Draw the character from the reference running through those positions. The pose
guide is an instruction, not artwork: its thin lines, its colours, its joint
dots, its white background and its blank circular head are NOT part of the
drawing and must not appear anywhere in it.

CAMERA: locked off. Identical distance and eye level in every frame. The
character must be exactly the same height in every frame, and the same height
as in the reference image — do not zoom, crop, recompose or rescale between
frames. All frames share one ground line: the sole of the planted foot touches
the same horizontal line in every frame.

VIEW: three-quarter view, running toward the left of frame, chest turned
slightly toward the viewer so the jersey number stays readable and reads
forwards. HIS HEAD AND FACE ARE TURNED TOWARD THE LEFT EDGE OF THE PICTURE, the
way he is running: his nose, his chin and his eyes all point that way, so his
face is seen in three-quarter view from his left-front. He is not looking at
the viewer and not looking back over his shoulder.

CRITICAL: he is DRIBBLING A BASKETBALL WHILE HE RUNS — this is not a plain
sprint. The hand on the VIEWER'S LEFT is the dribbling hand in frames 2 to 5.
It is always held out in front of his body with the palm facing DOWN toward the
floor, fingers spread, pushing an invisible ball down. It is never a fist,
never swung back, and never tucked in at his side. The OTHER arm does the
running, swinging freely.

FRAMES, left to right:
1. CALIBRATION POSE: standing straight upright, feet shoulder-width apart, arms
   hanging relaxed at his sides, facing the viewer, in the plain neutral
   standing pose from the reference image. This exact pose appears as the first
   frame of every sheet in this set and must be drawn identically every time.
2. Dribbling hand pushed down to the hem of his shorts, palm flat to the floor.
   Legs: the leg on the dribbling side forward and planted, the other leg
   stretched out behind him, its toe pushing off. Free arm swung forward across
   his chest.
3. Dribbling hand risen to the waistband of his shorts, palm still down. Legs
   mid-stride: the far foot planted under his body, and the leg NEARER THE
   VIEWER swinging through IN FRONT of it — that near knee comes up high and
   its shin crosses in front of his standing leg, so the whole swinging leg is
   plainly visible. Torso leaning forward.
4. Dribbling hand pushed down to the hem of his shorts again, palm flat down.
   Legs: the other leg forward and planted, the leg on the dribbling side
   stretched out behind him, its toe pushing off. Free arm swung back behind
   him.
5. Dribbling hand risen to the waistband of his shorts, palm down. Legs
   mid-stride the other way, and it must NOT repeat the pose of the earlier
   mid-stride frame: this time the NEAR foot is planted under his body and the
   leg FURTHER FROM THE VIEWER swings through BEHIND it, half hidden by his
   standing leg and his shorts — that far knee lifts less, and less of that leg
   shows.

This row is a seamless loop: frame 5 must flow back into frame 2 with no jump.

STYLE: VGA-era 256-colour DOS-game pixel art, drawn pixel by pixel — NOT a
modern illustration with a pixel filter over it. The limits below are the look;
keep all of them: - At most THREE tones per material: a base, one darker
shadow, one lighter highlight. Hard edges between the tones. - NO gradients, NO
soft or airbrushed shading, NO glow, NO bloom, and NO anti-aliasing anywhere —
not on the outline, not between tones, not around the silhouette. - Where a
tone change needs softening, use visible ORDERED DITHER — a checkerboard of the
two tones. Dither, never blend. - Chunky square pixels on one consistent grid,
plainly visible at full size. - A bold dark outline around the silhouette and
around the major forms inside it. The background must be fully transparent
(alpha 0) with no haze, glow or soft fringe around the silhouette. Output a
wide landscape image.

The character is NOT holding a basketball in any frame — the ball is drawn
separately by the game. His hand pushes down as if a ball were there.
